Art Institute of Chicago: The Sick Child I, his first color lithograph

highlight.text: Munch printed the lithograph with several different stones and a variety of color combinations: he made the keystone either black or red and added up to four other color stones in combinations of blue, gray, red, yellow, reddish brown, and purple-blue.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: Collection description: The Sick Child I (colour lithograph, 1896)

source.label: Wikipedia: in Paris he focused on graphic representations of his Frieze of Life themes

work.text: Due to the great success of the paintings and his own psychological preoccupations, in 1894–96 Munch made three prints based on the motif, of which The Sick Child I was the last. … There he made this, his first color lithograph, which features Sophie’s head silhouetted against a pillow.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: Collection description: The Sick Child I (colour lithograph, 1896)

work.text: Munch also produced multi-colored versions of The Sick Child, concerning tuberculosis, which sold well

moment.text: In Paris during the years 1896-97 Munch devoted most of his time to lithographic work and developed his [technique] of the coloured lithograph—probably inspired by [Toulouse-Lautrec]—in the workshop of the famous printer, Clot.

source.author: J. P. Hodin
source.title: “Edvard Munch's Graphic Art”, in Edvard Munch: Etchings, Woodcuts and Lithographs (exhibition catalogue)

moment.text: In 1896 the artist traveled to Paris to experiment with new print-making processes and work with respected printers such as Auguste Clot, hoping to gain the commercial success that had previously eluded him in the French capital.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: Collection description: The Sick Child I (colour lithograph, 1896)

matters.text: As for the sick child, it was the period I think of as the Age of the Pillow. A great many painters did pictures of sick children on their pillows.
matters.lead: Writing to the director of Oslo's National Gallery in 1930:

source.author: Edvard Munch
source.title: Letter to the director of the National Gallery, Oslo, 1930, quoted in “The Sick Child (Munch)”
source.license: Short excerpt of an English translation, via Wikipedia (CC BY-SA)

matters.text: Only someone who knew the conditions at home could possibly understand why there can be no conceivable chance of any other place having played a part – my home is to my art as a midwife is to her children

source.author: Edvard Munch
source.title: In conversation with Jens Thiis, c. 1933 (Munch Museum), as quoted in Sue Prideaux, Edvard Munch: Behind the Scream (2007), pp. 85–86, quoted on Wikiquote
